planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in early fall or just after spring bloom; 'Guinevere' forms slow-spreading clumps that benefit from division every three to four years.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, where its dark bronze-purple foliage shows best color. 'Guinevere' is an old cottage-garden primrose from the Garryarde strain, producing soft lilac-pink flowers with a small yellow eye held just above the crinkled, metallic-toned leaves in early to mid-spring. The bronze foliage remains attractive after bloom and provides useful color contrast at the front of a shaded border or woodland path all season. Keep soil evenly moist through the growing year and divide congested clumps right after flowering to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in early fall or immediately after spring bloom; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep plants vigorous.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to light sun. 'Captain Blood' is a long-cultivated cottage-garden primrose valued for its deep, velvety crimson-red flowers with a small yellow eye, carried just above low rosettes of crinkled green leaves from late winter into early spring. It is hardier and more tolerant of heavier soils than many modern primrose hybrids, making it a dependable choice for cottage borders, rock gardens, and shaded path edges. Keep the soil consistently moist through the growing season and lift and divide crowded clumps after flowering to renew vigor and increase stock.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in early fall; this double-flowered cultivar must be propagated by division to come true, since seedlings revert toward single flowers.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; 'Miss Indigo' is a double-flowered primrose cultivar whose fully packed, indigo-blue petals are edged in a fine silvery-white margin, giving each bloom a striking two-tone effect over neat rosettes of crinkled green leaves. Flowering runs from late winter into mid-spring and is heaviest in cool weather, slowing once summer heat arrives. Because it is a clonal double, propagate only by division of established clumps rather than by seed to keep the distinctive color and form true. Divide every two to three years after flowering to maintain vigor and prevent the center of the clump from dying out.

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in early fall; this historic double cultivar is propagated only by division and does not come true from seed.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; 'Alba Plena' is one of the oldest double primroses still in cultivation, producing fully packed, pure white, rosette-like flowers with no visible eye above neat clumps of crinkled green leaves in early to mid-spring. Its old-fashioned, cottage-garden character makes it a favorite for collectors of historic florists' flowers and a clean, bright accent against darker foliage in a shaded border. Divide clumps every two to three years immediately after flowering to maintain vigor, since this double form sets no viable seed and must be increased vegetatively. Keep soil consistently moist through spring and provide light shade in summer to avoid stress.

planting.note: Surface sow seed on moistened starting mix without covering, since seed needs light and cool temperatures to germinate; start 10-12 weeks before last frost or sow outdoors in late summer for natural stratification.

directions: Surface sow seed in cool conditions and grow on in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this wild subspecies of the common primrose, native to the Balkans, Caucasus, and parts of Turkey, differs from the familiar yellow European primrose in bearing flowers in shades of pink, magenta, or lilac-purple with the same yellow eye and crinkled rosette of leaves. It blooms very early, often among the first primroses to open in late winter, and naturalizes readily in cool, humus-rich woodland soil once established. Divide congested clumps every two to three years after flowering to maintain vigor and increase stock, and keep soil consistently moist through the spring growing season.

common_name: Apple Blossom Japanese Primrose (Pale Pink Candelabra Primrose)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil at the margin of a stream, pond, or bog in partial shade in spring.

directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade beside streams, ponds, or bog gardens. 'Apple Blossom' is a soft pale pink selection of Japanese candelabra primrose, carrying its gentle blush flowers in tiered whorls on upright stems from late spring through early summer, a lighter counterpoint to the more common crimson and magenta seed-grown forms. It self-sows modestly in reliably damp soil and combines well with deeper pink or white primrose selections for a graduated color display along a shaded water feature. Keep soil constantly moist through the growing season, since the plant goes dormant quickly if it dries out in summer heat.

common_name: Valley Red Japanese Primrose (Brick-Red Candelabra Primrose)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil at the margin of a stream, pond, or bog in partial shade in spring.

directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade beside streams, ponds, or bog gardens. 'Valley Red' is a classic named selection of Japanese candelabra primrose chosen for its deep brick-red flowers, carried in the same stacked, tiered whorls on tall stems as the species from late spring into early summer. Isolating plantings from other color forms helps self-sown seedlings stay true to the deep red color, since open pollination with other shades produces mixed results. Pair with ferns, hostas, and astilbes in a permanently moist, partially shaded water-garden setting, and expect foliage to die back completely in hot, dry summer weather.

common_name: Cowichan Group Polyanthus Primrose (Self-Colored Velvet Primrose Strain)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 14-16 weeks before last frost after surface-sowing and cold-stratifying at 35-40F for 3-4 weeks; transplant into partial shade after hardening off.

directions: Surface-sow tiny seed on moist, sterile mix and cold-stratify at 35-40F for 3-4 weeks before germinating at cooler room temperature, then transplant into moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade. The Cowichan Group is an old polyanthus primrose strain, historically associated with Vancouver Island's Cowichan Valley, prized for rich, velvety self-colored flowers in garnet, wine, blue, or purple that lack the pale central eye-zone typical of most polyanthus primroses. It blooms heavily in cool spring weather over neat rosettes of crinkled leaves, then slows or goes dormant once summer heat arrives. Divide congested clumps after flowering to maintain named colors true, since open-pollinated seedlings from mixed plantings can drift back toward eyed forms.

common_name: Ruby Drumstick Primrose (Deep Red Drumstick Primrose)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in early fall; like the species, 'Ruby' goes semi-dormant in summer heat and prefers drier conditions once flowering finishes.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; 'Ruby' is a deep red-flowered selection of drumstick primrose, producing the same perfectly spherical flower heads on upright stalks as the species but in a rich wine-red rather than the typical purple, lilac, or pink shades. It brightens shady woodland edges in early to mid-spring and pairs well with the white 'Alba' form for a strong color contrast in a mixed drift. Keep soil consistently moist through the spring growing season, and divide congested clumps right after flowering to maintain vigor and keep the deep red color true, since seed-grown plants do not come reliably red.

common_name: Grandiflora Drumstick Primrose (Large-Flowered Purple Drumstick Primrose)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in early fall; like the species, 'Grandiflora' goes semi-dormant in summer heat and prefers drier conditions once flowering finishes.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; 'Grandiflora' is a large-flowered selection of drumstick primrose, producing oversized, densely packed, spherical purple flower heads on sturdy upright stalks that are noticeably bigger than the species' typical blooms. The bold, rounded flower heads create a strong architectural accent against the coarsely toothed, wrinkled rosette of leaves in early to mid-spring. Keep soil consistently moist through the spring growing season and provide light mulch in cold climates, and divide congested clumps right after flowering to maintain vigor and increase stock true to type.
